The question of whether a person can be harmed by an event that occurs after their death is a complex and debated topic among philosophers. I will argue that it is coherent to say that a person can be harmed by an event that occurs after their death, and I will explore the implications of this position on wills and posthumous reputation.

My argument is based on the idea that harm is not solely limited to physical or psychological damage that occurs during a person's lifetime. Rather, harm can also be understood as a violation of a person's interests, rights, or dignity, which can persist even after their death. In the case of a broken promise made to a deceased person, the harm lies in the fact that the promise was not fulfilled, which can be seen as a betrayal of the trust and expectations that the person had placed in the promisor.

For example, imagine that a person had made a promise to a friend to take care of their family after their death, but the friend fails to do so. Even though the person is no longer alive to experience the consequences of the broken promise, it can still be argued that they have been harmed by the friend's failure to fulfill their obligation. The harm lies in the fact that the person's trust and expectations were not respected, and that their wishes were not carried out.

This position implies that wills and posthumous reputation are not just mere formalities, but rather have a significant impact on the well-being and dignity of the deceased person. A will, for instance, is a document that reflects a person's wishes and intentions regarding the distribution of their property and the care of their loved ones after their death. If a will is not respected or is contested, it can be seen as a harm to the deceased person's interests and wishes.

Similarly, a person's posthumous reputation can be harmed if they are slandered, defamed, or misrepresented after their death. Even though the person is no longer alive to experience the harm, their reputation and legacy can still be damaged, which can have a significant impact on their loved ones and the way they are remembered.

In conclusion, I argue that it is coherent to say that a person can be harmed by an event that occurs after their death, such as the breaking of a promise made to them. This position implies that wills and posthumous reputation are important aspects of a person's well-being and dignity, and that they should be respected and protected even after the person's death. It also highlights the importance of fulfilling obligations and promises made to the deceased, and of treating their legacy and reputation with respect and dignity.

Ultimately, this position recognizes that a person's interests, rights, and dignity do not cease to exist at the moment of their death, but rather can persist and be affected by events that occur after their passing. This perspective encourages us to think more carefully about the impact of our actions on the deceased and their loved ones, and to strive to act with respect, integrity, and compassion in our dealings with the dead.
